newsitem.title: USA: Delta, Continental decline comment on merger reports.
newsitem.headline: Delta, Continental decline comment on merger reports.

text.p: Continental Airlines and Delta Air Lines were mum Wednesday about published reports that they have held talks on a merger that would create the world's largest airline.
"It is our policy not to comment on rumour and speculation in the marketplace," said a spokesman for Houston-based Continental, the nation's No. 5 airline.
"It is our long-standing policy that we do not respond to questions about mergers, acquisitions, takeovers or major investments," Delta spokesman Bill Berry said.

The New York Times and Wall Street Journal, both quoting sources familiar with the discussions, reported that the two companies have been talking about a merger for several months. The Times said that a deal was not imminent.
Atlanta-based Delta is the nation's third-largest airline.

A merger of the two carriers would probably spark another round of consolidation in the airline industry, which has recovered to post solid earnings this year and last after struggling for much of the prior decade.

USAir Group put itself up for sale a year ago and held talks with United Airlines, the nation's largest carrier, and No. 2 American Airlines. But the talks were later called off. United Airlines is a unit of UAL Corp., and American is owned by AMR Corp.

While giving no expected value for a deal, the Wall Street Journal noted that Continental's most widely traded stock was worth about $1.8 billion at the closing price of $28.375 for the class B shares on Tuesday.
The class B stock jumped $1.625 to $30 on the New York Stock Exchange after the reports. Delta stock added 12.5 cents to $75.125, also on the NYSE.
The reports, stating Continental had initiated the talks, also noted that several Continental executives had sold blocks of the company's stock recently.

In a memo sent to employees Wednesday, Continental's two top executives said they had exercised stock options for year-end tax and investment purposes, and would not have sold shares if a merger were imminent.

"We would obviously not have exercised stock options if we thought a merger was around the corner which would create a windfall for all stockholders," Chairman Gordon Bethune and President Greg Brenneman said.
In the memo, a copy of which was obtained by Reuters, the executives said the airline was constantly assessing options in the event of an industry consolidation.

"Should an industry consolidation occur, and we are not saying it will, Continental will only be involved in a manner which is fair to both our Continental co-workers and our shareholders," the executives said in the memo.
Continental and Delta combined would fly about a quarter of the nation's airline passengers, compared with about 21 percent for Chicago-based United.

Continental and Delta would fit well geographically, with Continental strong in Houston, the New York area and Latin and central America, and Delta's strength concentrated in the Southeast, along the East Coast and in Europe.
